title: Definition
body_md:
A node $j$ of a graph is a soft node for an eigenvalue
$\lambda$ of the graph Laplacian if there exists an eigenvector
$\mathbf{v}$ for this eigenvalue such that $v_j = 0$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $\lambda$ be an eigenvalue of $G$ for eigenvector $\mathbf{x}$ { for the matrix $L$.} If $x_i = x_j$, 
then $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $G^{\prime}$ for $\mathbf{x}$, where $G^{\prime}$ is
the graph obtained from G by deleting or adding $e = \{i, j\}$ 
depending on whether or not it is an edge of G.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $\lambda$ be an eigenvalue of G for eigenvector $\mathbf{x}$ for the matrix 
$Q$. If $x_i = -x_j$, 
then $\lambda $ is an eigenvalue of $G^{\prime}$ for $\mathbf{x}$, where $G^{\prime}$ is
the graph obtained from G by deleting or adding $e = \{i, j\}$ 
depending on whether or not it is an edge of G.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For a vertex $i$ we have 
$$d_i x_i + \sum_{k \sim i} x_k = \lambda x_i,$$
where $d_i$ is the degree of $i$.
Assume there is a vertex $j$ such that $x_i = -x_j$ and let us add the edge
$e = \{i, j\}$ to $G$ to form $G^{\prime}$. Then for $G'$ we have
$$(d_i+1) x_i + \sum_{k \sim i} x_k - x_i = d_i x_i + \sum_{k \sim i} x_k=\lambda x_i,$$
and the proof is complete.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $\lambda$ be an eigenvalue of G for eigenvector $\mathbf{x}$ for the matrix 
$A$ and let two vertices $i$ and $j$ such that $x_i = x_j =0$, 
then $\lambda $ is an eigenvalue of $G^{\prime}$ for $\mathbf{x}$, where $G^{\prime}$ is
the graph obtained from G by deleting or adding $e = \{i, j\}$ 
depending on whether or not it is an edge of G.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Without loss of generality, consider two nonadjacent vertices $i$ and $j$.  
For $i$ and $j$ we have 
$$ \sum_{k \sim i} x_k = \lambda x_i ,$$
and 
$$ \sum_{k \sim j} x_k = \lambda x_j.$$
Adding an edge $ij$, if we still have $\mathbf{x}$ as an eigenvector of the new matrix for the same eigenvalue, then the eigenvalue equations read:
$$ x_j + \sum_{k \sim i, k \neq j} x_k = \lambda x_i,$$
$$ x_i + \sum_{k \sim j, k \neq i} x_k = \lambda x_j,$$
This holds if and only if both $x_i=0$ and $x_j=0$. In this case, the eigenvalue equations for the other vertices are unaffected.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $\mathbf{x}$ be an eigenvector of G affording $\lambda$ { for the matrix $L.$}
Suppose the vertices in $Z = \{k \in V(G): x(k) \neq 0\}$ can be paired 
up in such a way that if i and j are paired vertices then $x_i = -x_j$. 
Suppose further that all paired vertices in Z are adjacent (not adjacent) to 
each other. Let $G^{\prime}$ be the graph
obtained from G by removing (resp. adding new) edges between all paired vertices of
Z. Then $\mathbf{x}$  is an eigenvector of $G^{\prime}$ for $\lambda - 2$ 
(resp. for $\lambda + 2$).
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $\mathbf{x}$ be an eigenvector of G affording $\lambda$ {for the matrix $Q$.}
Suppose the vertices in $Z = \{k \in V(G): x(k) \neq 0\}$ can be paired 
up in such a way that if i and j are paired vertices then $x_i = x_j$. 
Suppose further that all paired vertices in Z are adjacent (not adjacent) to 
each other. Let $G^{\prime}$ be the graph
obtained from G by removing (resp. adding new) edges between all paired vertices of
Z. Then $\mathbf{x}$  is an eigenvector of $G^{\prime}$ for $\lambda - 2$ 
(resp. for $\lambda + 2$).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We consider adding a matching; the proof when deleting a matching is similar.
    Let vertex $i \in Z,$ and the corresponding pair $j$ such that $x_{i} = x_{j} \ne 0.$ The Laplacian eigenequation to vertex $i$ in $G^{\prime}$ given by 
\begin{eqnarray}
(d_i+1) x_{i} +\sum_{ \{k,i\} \, \in \,  E(G^{\prime}) } x_{k}  &=& d_i x_{i} + x_{i} + \sum_{\{k,i\} \in E(G) } x_{k} + x_{j} \nonumber \\
&=& \lambda \, x_{i} + x_{i} + x_{j}.
\end{eqnarray}
Since $x_{i} = x_{j},$ then 
$$
(d_i+1) x_{i}+ \sum_{\{i,j\} \in E(G^{\prime}) } x_{j}  = (\lambda+2) \, x_{i},
$$
and the proof is complete.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{addQ}
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph affording an 
eigenvalue $\lambda \neq 0$ for $L$ or $Q$ for an eigenvector { $\mathbf{x}$ with $\sum_i x_i = 0$.} Then 
the new graph $G'$ obtained by adding
a node connected to all the nodes of $G$ has eigenvalue $\lambda +1$
for the eigenvector $\mathbf{x}^{\prime}$ obtained by extending $\mathbf{x}$ by a zero component.

title: Theorem
body_md:
Assume a graph $G=(V,E)$ with $n$ vertices where
$\mathbf{x}$ is an eigenvector of L, Q or A such that $x_i=0$ for an eigenvalue $\lambda$
and a vertex $i$. The graph $G'$ where we add a vertex $k$ connected to $i$
has the eigenvector $(\mathbf{x},0)^T$ for the eigenvalue $\lambda$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $Q$
$$d_i x_i + \sum_{j \sim i} x_j = \lambda x_i.$$
Assume $x_i=0$ and adding vertex $k$ such that $x_k=0$ we get
$$(d_i+1)\cdot  0  + \sum_{j \sim i} x_j +0 = 0 = \lambda x_i.$$
{ For vertex $k$, we have 
$$x_{k} + x_{i} = 0 = \lambda x_{k}.$$
}

The proof is trivially extended to $A$.

title: Proposition
body_md: Let $P_n$ be a path on $n \geq 3$ vertices. Then, $P_n$ is not $A$-bivalent.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write the vertex set of $P_n$ as $V = S \cup \overline{S}$ such that $S \cap \overline{S} = \emptyset.$  Let $u \in V$ be a leaf, $v \sim u$ and $w \sim v.$ \\
\noindent Consider the following cases: 

\noindent \textit{Case 1:} Let $u \in S$ and $v \in \overline{S}:$ note that 
$$d_u(S) - d_u(S,\overline{S}) = \lambda_A = -1.$$
Now, let $w \sim v$. If $w \in \overline{S},$ then $d_v(\overline{S}) - d_v(\overline{S}, S) = \lambda_A = 0,$ which is a contradiction. If $w \in S,$ we obtain $d_v(\overline{S}) - d_v(\overline{S}, S) = \lambda_A = -2,$ which is a contradiction.

\noindent  \textit{Case 2:} Let $u, v \in S:$ in this case, 
$$d_u(S) - d_u(S,\overline{S}) = \lambda_A = 1.$$ If $w \in \overline{S},$ then $d_v(S) - d_v(S, \overline{S}) = \lambda_A = 0,$ which is a contradiction. If $w \in S,$ then $d_v(S) - d_v(S, \overline{S}) = \lambda_A = 2,$ which is a contradiction. 
Therefore, there are no $A$-bivalent paths for $n\geq 3$.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md: Let $P_n$ be a path on $n \geq 4$ vertices. Then, $P_n$ is $Q$-bivalent associated with $\lambda_{Q} = 0$ for any $n$ and $Q$-bivalent associated with $\lambda_{Q} = 2$ when $n$ is even.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It is clear from Lemma \ref{lem:Qbip}, that $\lambda_{Q} = 0$ is associated with a $Q$-bivalent eigenvector, and the first case is proved for any $n$ { $\geq 4 $}.  

Now, let $P_{n}: e_1\, e_2\,\ldots e_{n-1}$ where $e_{i}=(v_{i}, v_{i+1})$ is an edge connecting vertices $v_i$ and $v_{i+1}.$ There are two ways of arranging the  vertices of $P_n$ in the sets $S$ and $\overline{S}$. 
First, consider that we arrange the edges of $P_n$ such that there are no edges between the vertices of $S$ and no edges between the vertices of $\overline{S}$. This is exactly the same case as the previous one, which was already proved. Second, we can arrange the edges such that $e_{2k+1} \in S$ and $e_{2k+3} \in \overline{S}.$ If $n$ is even, then the graphs induced by $S$ and $\overline{S}$ are unions of paths $P_2.$ From Theorem \ref{thmAL21}, $P_n$ is $Q$-bivalent associated with $\lambda_{Q} = 2.$ If $n$ is odd, then one of the two graphs induced by $S$ or $\overline{S}$  is a union of paths $P_2$ and the other one is a union of paths $P_2$ and an isolated vertex. From Theorem \ref{thmAL21}, this is a contradiction, and the result follows.

label: prop310
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop310}
Let $T$ be a tree on $n$ vertices. If $T$ is $A$-bivalent, the bivalent eigenvector is associated with eigenvalues $\lambda_A=1$ or $\lambda_A=-1.$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $v$ be a leaf of $T$ and $u$ its neighbor. If $u$ and $v$ are in the same set, say $S$, then $d_{v}(S) - d_{v}(S,\overline{S}) = \lambda_A = 1.$ Since $T$ is $A$-bivalent, from Theorem \ref{thmAL21}, we should arrange all vertices of $T$ such that this same equation is true for $\lambda_A=1.$ Then, $\lambda_A = 1.$ 
If $v$ and $u$ are in different sets, then 
$d_{v}(S) - d_{v}(S,\overline{S}) = \lambda_A = -1.$ Using the same previous argument, this equation should be true for all vertices of the tree, that is, $\lambda_A=-1,$ and the result follows.
head: environment

label: lemma:1
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\noindent Write the vertex set of $T$ as $V = S \cup \overline{S}$ such that $S \cap \overline{S} = \emptyset.$ \\ 
\noindent (a)  Suppose that $u \in S$ and $v \in \overline{S} $ are two leaves of $T$ incident to the same vertex. Let $w \sim u$. In this case,
$d_u(S) - d_u(S, \overline{S}) = \lambda_A = -1.$ On the other hand, 
$d_v(\overline{S}) - d_u( \overline{S}, S) = \lambda_A = 1,$ which is a contradiction.

\noindent (b) Let $uv$ be an edge in $S$ such that $d_{u}(T) = 2$ and $d_{v}(T) = 1,$ and let $w \in N(u).$ Note that  
$d_u(S) - d_u(S, \overline{S}) = \lambda_A \in \{0,2\}$ depending whether $w$ is in $\overline{S}$ or $S$. On the other hand, 
$d_v(S) - d_v(S, \overline{S}) = \lambda_A = 1,$ which is a contradiction.

\noindent (c) for a leaf $v \in S, \;   d_{v}(S) - d_{v}(S,\overline{S}) = \lambda_A \in \{-1,1\}.$ For $w \in S, \; d_{w}(S) - d_{w}(S,\overline{S}) = \lambda_A \geq 2,$ which is a contradiction.

label: thm:odddegree
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:odddegree}
    If a tree $T$ on $n$ vertices is $A$-bivalent then all of its vertices are of odd degree. Moreover, $n$ is even.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider a tree $T$ with an $A$-eigenvector $\mathbf{x}$ affording an eigenvalue $\lambda_A$. We already know from Proposition \ref{prop310} that  $\lambda_A =1$ or $\lambda_A =-1$. 
Then the eigenvalue equation reads : 
$$
\sum_{j \sim i} x_j = \lambda_A x_i \qquad \forall i \in V.
$$
This implies that any vertex will have an odd number of adjacent vertices, with a difference of 1 in the count of $1's$ and -$1's.$ 
Also, since the sum of the vertex degrees of a graph is even and each vertex of the tree has odd degree, then $n$ should be even.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The reciprocal of Theorem \ref{thm:odddegree} is not true. See for instance the graph $K_{1,2k+1}$ for any integer $k$, which is not $A$-bivalent.
